items.title: X Window System on the ESP32
items.summary: There are a lot of things you can do with an Xserver, but run it on a microcontroller? Well, if that microcontroller is an ESP32-S3, [Sergey Zorin]– and Claude– have got you covered with Woodland X11 , a full-featured port of everyone’s favourite XServer. Now, it is just the core Xserver with no extensions, and currently targeted specifically at the Elecrow CrowPanel Advance 4.3″, a device that packages an ESP32-S3-N16R8 with an 800×480 RGB565 IPS panel and GT911 touch. In this implementation, your finger is the Xcursor. There’s even two-finger scroll implemented, though no keyboard. As you can see in the demo video embedded below, it works well enough for those oldschool X applications like xclock, xcalc and– crucially!– xeyes. What’s the point of an Xserver without googly eyes, anyway? In reality, you’re not likely to set this up just for Xeyes, but the idea of having bringing Linux applications to a little display via WiFi or — as in the video– wired connection has no limit of use cases. Try that with Wayland ! Considering X11’s vintage, it is perhaps not surprising that it fits on the ESP32-S3, a chip we’ve seen emulate an entire 386 PC before– a PC that could run an Xserver, for you youngun’s. items.title: Using a Toothbrush’s NFC chip to Unlock a Computer
items.summary: Depending on which type of electric toothbrush you are using, the replaceable brushes may contain an NFC chip that the handle and possibly base station uses to track various details, such as time spent brushing and when to replace the brush. The Philips Sonicare of [Circuit Helper] is one such unit, with its NFC chip tracking aspects like runtime and pressure . Unsurprisingly it’s easy enough to read and write this same NFC chip with a PN532 NFC reader and ESP32-S3 MCU. This reveals data fields for everything from brush type, to total runtime and expected lifetime, inviting a bit of experimentation on how certain usage patterns affects these data fields. This much is perhaps not too shocking, but the fun part is what you can do with the chip after you have figured out how to write to its memory. How to unlock these units and their NXP NTAG213 IC has been figured out a few years ago already, so the hardest part was to figure out what to do with this information. The demonstrated use case in the video is to unlock an Apple Macbook, which is maybe a bit too niche. Also demonstrated is taking the chip and its antenna out of the brush, which turns out to be quite easy. items.title: Fixing a Dead Socket LGA 1851 Mainboard with a Resistor
items.summary: Doing board level diagnosis on a PCB is hardly black magic, but some PCBs are definitely more daunting than others. The Socket LGA 1851 mainboard that [Fix the Pixel] got in for repair being one of the harder cases due to the sheer size and complexity. Adding to the excitement was having to purchase a used CPU for it off eBay to even test the board and work through the boot-up sequence to find the culprit. A basic understanding of how these mainboards power up and verify that they can move on to the next phase is essential here, starting with the power rails. Although the culprit turned out to be a single missing 5.1 Ohm resistor on an SPI clock line, you still have to reason your way through the diagnosis. For this mainboard the boardview was fortunately available, but that still doesn’t make it easy to spot components that have quietly left the chat. With the CPU and RAM installed the board doesn’t bother to boot up, with the VRM controller for the CPU’s power phases showing its enable pin to stay low. Going down the list of conditions for this pin to be pulled high the culprit was eventually found, when the PCH – the board’s chipset – never reading the BIOS chip. Checking the SPI lines on the mainboard near the BIOS chip quickly showed the knocked-off resistor on the SPI clock line. Soldering a fresh resistor in place resulted in the board happily booting up once more. Although having a boardview here available helps a lot, checking such basics like the SPI line resistors around the BIOS can be a quick checklist item before dragging out the big diagnostics guns or shelling out money for a boardview file. But every autumn, I would pick up dozens of them from the sidewalks of Sofia and fill my pockets — not as a spell against fear but as an ode to joy. Conkers, as the English call them, spun me up in delight — shiny as mahogany, smooth as river stones, tiny planets from some other universe, the wonder-smitten eyes of some prehistoric creature. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
items.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.
